codex.section: §5.6 Entry-state analysis, rule 1; §2 effective control context; §8.3 own versus total controls

steps.claim: §5.6 first disables an operation when an “effective control” is known false, then makes an X-family target unknown unless all operands are known. §2 defines the effective control context as active predicates plus inherited controls, and §8.3 distinguishes these from a gate’s own controls. §5.6 forbids a stronger analysis from narrowing D_F.
steps.by: clause:ISA-5.6 (entry-state rule 1 and opening paragraph); clause:ISA-2-P10; clause:ISA-8.3

steps.claim:
Use a perm_action with interface t:wire mut and u:wire in, no arguments, bounds or memory, and this complete body after ^entry():
z = qalloc any 1
c = qalloc any 1
ccx z u c
b = qborrow any 1
cx c b
qreturn b
ccx z u c
qfree c
qfree z
The current reference check accepted this object through /dev/stdin, returning status ok. It used the 0.8 header and signature abi under the binding erratum; the probe interface hash was eb30a43722acc6c124c4c4bea0e3649915b964ea4e08806933e96cc4c37581f6 and object hash 64de1ae460626ce409f99b798e654b3c9bf05b3a9d53ded0fdb93a0a416f019c. No file or repository modification was needed.

On the literal contextual-control reading, ccx z u c has an empty effective control context. Since u is unknown, not all operands are known, so the rule makes c unknown. At the subsequent single-gate frame, D_F includes c=1,b=0; cx c b sends b to 1. No P′ acting independently of B can satisfy the required identity on B over that domain. The later cleanup does not repair a failed individual frame obligation.
steps.by: step:<1>1; step:<1>2; clause:ISA-5.6 (Cartesian-product domain and restricted factorisation)

steps.claim: The reference tests all controls, including the explicit z operand of ccx. It skips the operation because z=0, retaining c=0, and the frame is identity on its resulting domain {c=0} × {b=0,1}. This explains the observed admission and agrees with the intended known-false transfer, but is stronger than the contextual-control reading of rule 1.

Thus the published control terminology and the aligned reference lead to different D_F and different validity decisions for one finite object. This is an S0 normative admission ambiguity, rather than a choice of proof format or a missing optimisation; both candidate domains conservatively contain the reachable entry state.

codex.problem: Rule 1 does not explicitly include the operation’s own controls in the known-false shortcut, although the reference does. Elsewhere the specification distinguishes own controls from effective control context. With a known-false own control and another unknown operand, the literal rule loses a local constant that the reference retains; because D_F is normative and cannot be narrowed by stronger analysis, this changes acceptance of a borrow frame.
codex.fix: In §5.6 rule 1, replace “An effective control known false disables the operation.” with: “If any control literal is known false, counting the operation’s own controls together with its effective control context, the operation is disabled: preserve all abstract values and record no causal event.” Keep the existing all-operands-known rule after this shortcut. Add the body in step <1>2 as a suite F/frame_domain case with expected acceptance and c=0 at frame entry. The alternative is to restrict the reference shortcut to contextual controls and require this object to fail; I recommend the text repair because it preserves the implemented, sound known-false analysis and the maintainer’s chosen admission boundary.
